title: Your Mother Died With a $3,000 Social Security Benefit. Could You Qualify to Collect Up to 75%?
summary: You could qualify for up to 75% of your mother’s $3,000 Social Security benefit, but only if you meet a few strict conditions.
body_markdown:
If your mother had a $3,000 Social Security benefit, it might seem natural to collect part of it after she dies. Survivor benefits for children, however, come with strict rules and typically exclude adults. Here’s how you may be able to claim up to 75% ($2,250 a month) and why Social Security’s family limit could reduce that amount.


## Who Can Collect Survivor Benefits on a Parent’s Record


[Social Security limits survivor benefits](https://smartasset.com/financial-advisor/social-security-survivor-benefits) on a deceased parent’s record to certain children. Biological and adopted children may qualify, while stepchildren and grandchildren must meet additional requirements.


Being an adult child isn’t enough on its own. If you’re over 19 and not disabled, you generally can’t receive a[child survivor benefit](https://smartasset.com/financial-advisor/survivor-benefits-for-children) , even if your parent was[getting Social Security](https://smartasset.com/retirement/social-security-calculator) at the time of death. The table shows which children may qualify and typical end dates for payments:1


Your Situation Eligibility Requirement Benefits Generally End


Minor child Unmarried and under 18 At age 18


High school student Ages 18 to 19 and enrolled full time in grade 12 or below At graduation or two months after turning 19, whichever is first


Disabled adult child Disability began before age 22 If you no longer meet the disability or other eligibility rules


**A[financial advisor](https://smartasset.com/retirement/find-a-financial-planner?utm_source=smartasset&utm_medium=google_discover_referral&utm_campaign=dp_social_security&utm_content=motherdiedwith3000socialsecuritybenefitcouldqualifytocollectupto75percent_a) can help you create an estate plan that keeps your children financially secure if you die.**


## How Much You Could Get Under the Family Maximum


An eligible child may receive up to 75% of the deceased parent’s[primary insurance amount (PIA)](https://smartasset.com/retirement/what-is-social-security-benefit-based-on) . This is the benefit your parent would have gotten at[full retirement age (FRA)](https://smartasset.com/retirement/full-retirement-age) . For example, a $3,000 PIA could provide $2,250 monthly ($3,000 × 75%), or $27,000 annually.


A parent’s PIA may differ from the amount deposited each month. As an example, if your parent claimed at 62 and their monthly payment was $2,100, the PIA could still have been $3,000. Your[survivor benefit](https://smartasset.com/retirement/husband-died-here-is-how-much-of-his-social-security-i-can-claim) would be calculated from the higher figure. Social Security can confirm the correct amount.


Social Security also caps the total paid to family members on one worker’s record. The family maximum is determined using a formula based on the worker’s PIA.


For 2027, a $3,000 PIA would set the family maximum at about $5,341. The formula applies 150% to the first $1,712, 272% to the next $759 and 134% to the remaining $529.2 The table shows how this family maximum could affect payments as more children qualify:


Eligible Children Combined Benefits Before the Cap Family Maximum Monthly Benefit per Child


One $2,250 $5,341 $2,250


Two $4,500 ($2,250 × 2) $5,341 $2,250


Three $6,750 ($2,250 × 3) $5,341 About $1,780 ($5,341 ÷ 3)


In this example, adding a third eligible child would lower each payment by about $470 a month ($2,250 − $1,780). A[surviving spouse](https://smartasset.com/financial-advisor/financial-planning-for-widows) drawing benefits from the same record can also affect the amounts available under the cap.


## How to Apply After a Parent Dies


Survivor benefits generally require an application, so you or[your guardian](https://smartasset.com/financial-advisor/conservatorship-vs-guardianship) may need to contact Social Security. You can apply by phone or at a local Social Security office. Filing promptly can help avoid delays or the loss of benefits for months that aren’t payable retroactively.


A new application may not be necessary if you were already entitled to child benefits on the parent’s record before the death.3 Social Security can confirm whether you need to file a claim.


Gather your parent’s[Social Security number](https://smartasset.com/financial-advisor/social-security-number) and a copy of the death certificate, along with documents showing your identity, age and relationship to your parent, such as a birth or adoption record. Students may need proof of enrollment, while disability claims can require medical records.


Once payments begin, report changes that could affect eligibility, such as graduation, leaving school or a change in disability status. A[financial advisor](https://smartasset.com/retirement/find-a-financial-planner?utm_source=smartasset&utm_medium=google_discover_referral&utm_campaign=dp_social_security&utm_content=motherdiedwith3000socialsecuritybenefitcouldqualifytocollectupto75percent_a) can help your family build a budget around survivor benefits until they end.
